question: to the Commission Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE), Isabella Lövin (Verts/ALE) Subject:

On 11 June 2026, the President of the Commission received a copy of a letter of concern sent by Nordic nature conservation societies to the Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). The letter raises deep concern about unsustainable fishing quotas and destructive fishing practices in protected marine areas – issues linked to several specific articles of the Convention – as well as to specific targets of the Global Biodiversity Framework adopted under the Kunming-Montreal Agreement. The letter considered that although ‘the EU is committed to the full and swift implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework’1 it is neither fulfilling obligations within the Convention itself, nor ensuring sufficient progress in reaching the relevant Kunming Montreal targets: 1.

How will the Commission change fisheries and ocean management using an ecosystem approach to guarantee that the EU can meet the obligations under the CBD to halt biodiversity loss and restore ocean health?
How will the Commission guarantee that destructive bottom-trawl fishing will not take place in Natura 2000 areas in the future, so obligations and targets under the CBD can be met?
https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/nature-and-biodiversity/global-biodiversity_en.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.8.2026) The Commission is fully committed to achieving the EU’s marine biodiversity objectives to contribute to the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework as can be seen in the Convention on Biological Diversity online reporting tool. The EU implements the ecosystem-based approach through the Birds1, Habitats2, Marine Strategy Framework3 and the Maritime Spatial Planning4 Directives, the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP)5, the Nature Restoration Regulation6 and the Biodiversity Strategy7. The Commission regularly assesses progress in achieving marine protection and sustainable fisheries objectives under EU law. The recently launched OceanEye8 will support the development of a strong evidence base for sustainable marine management. Under the Habitats Directive, Member States must prevent deterioration of protected habitats and species and adopt conservation objectives and measures for each Natura 2000 site. They must assess, case by case, whether fishing activities, including mobile bottom-contacting gears, are compatible with the corresponding conservation objectives. Under the Marine Action Plan9 the Commission sets out its vision on how to best preserve marine biodiversity and increase the resilience and sustainability of fisheries, exploiting synergies between the CFP and the environmental legislation. It issued a guidance on Natura 2000 and fishing10. The European Ocean Pact11 addresses sustainability and protecting and restoring ocean health. Under the Nature Restoration Regulation, Member States are required to restore degraded marine habitats, which may involve restrictions on mobile bottom fishing. Member States are due to submit their first national restoration plans in September 2026.
